title: A GRACE Interatomic Potential for W--Ta Systems: Application to Ta Segregation and Pinning of Shear-Coupled Grain-Boundary Migration
authors: Omar Hussein, Laurent Capolungo, Danny Perez
abstract: Tungsten-tantalum alloys are promising plasma-facing materials for fusion reactors, but simulations of their coupled defect, mechanical, and microstructural evolution require an interatomic potential that remains accurate across diverse atomic environments. We develop a transferable W-Ta potential within the GRaph Atomic Cluster Expansion (GRACE) framework. The primary training dataset was generated automatically by maximizing information entropy in an atomically relevant feature space, avoiding manual enumeration of the structures and processes required for specific downstream applications. Extensive validation demonstrates a consistent description of unary and binary phase stability, elasticity, phonons, high-pressure response, surfaces, point defects, dislocation energetics, transformation pathways, alloy thermodynamics, and melting behavior.   As a demonstration, the potential is applied to Ta segregation and shear-coupled migration of a $\Sigma5(120)$ W GB. Simulations reveal strongly site-selective segregation: Ta preferentially occupies a small subset of crystallographically distinct atomic rows. Under shear, segregated Ta impedes disconnection-mediated grain boundary migration. The de-pinning stress initially increases with Ta concentration but plateaus as the dominant pinning environment becomes saturated, while increasing temperature weakens both segregation and pinning. These results establish a broadly validated W-Ta potential and demonstrate how automated entropy-maximized data generation can produce transferable atomistic models capable of resolving mechanisms not explicitly targeted during training.
summary: This work introduces and validates a novel, highly transferable interatomic potential (GRACE) for W-Ta alloys using an entropy-maximized training methodology. The potential is shown to accurately predict numerous bulk and defect properties of the system. Applying this model, the authors successfully simulate how Ta segregates to grain boundaries and subsequently pins the boundary's migration under shear stress.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an accurate, transferable interatomic potential for W-Ta alloys to simulate complex coupled defect, mechanical, and microstructural evolution relevant to fusion reactors.
main_result: The developed GRACE potential accurately describes various physical properties, and simulations demonstrate that Ta segregation at grain boundaries impedes grain boundary migration, a process whose de-pinning stress plateaus upon saturation.
method: The authors developed a Graph Atomic Cluster Expansion (GRACE) potential trained using an information entropy maximization approach on DFT-generated data, which was then validated across numerous physical properties.
model_or_system: The system under study is Tungsten-Tantalum (W-Ta) alloys, modeled using the GRACE interatomic potential. The potential is validated across BCC W and Ta, covering properties like elasticity, defect energetics, and phase stability.
key_observables: De-pinning stress, Ta segregation patterns (site-selectivity), lattice constants, cohesive energies, elastic constants, and phonon dispersion relations.
important_parameters: Temperature (influencing segregation/pinning), Ta concentration, and the specific crystallographic nature of the grain boundary ($\Sigma5(120)$).
main_assumptions: The key assumption is that the entropy-maximized training data leads to a potential that is highly transferable, allowing it to predict mechanisms not explicitly included in the training set.
figures_summary: Figures compare the predictive accuracy of GRACE against other potentials (EAM/FS, GEAM) for energies and forces, and show the effect of temperature on segregation/pinning.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for accurate potentials for W-Ta systems. It details the GRACE potential development using entropy maximization and validates it against a wide range of DFT-calculated properties (unary/binary stability, elasticity, defects). Finally, it applies the potential to simulate Ta segregation and its effect on grain boundary migration.
why_interesting: While focused on materials science, the core methodology—using machine learning (GRACE) trained on high-dimensional, entropy-maximized data to achieve transferability across diverse physical regimes—is highly relevant to developing ML potentials for complex quantum many-body systems.

The columns correspond to (a,d) W, (b,e) Ta, and (c,f) mixed W–Ta configurations. Counts are plotted on a logarithmic scale, and the annotations report the number of samples N, mean µ, and standard deviation σ for each distribution.

Figure 2: Parity plots comparing DFT energies and atomic force components with predictions from GRACE, EAM/FS, and GEAM for W, Ta, and W–Ta configurations. Panels (a)–(c) show shifted energies per atom, and panels (d)–(f) show force components. Dashed lines indicate perfect agreement with DFT.
Figure 3: Equation-of-state curves for competing crystal structures of pure (a) W and (b) Ta predicted by the GRACE potential.
